title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 10: Bannes — no real independence; Apage — glory with future good works
pass_a_gloss: The very same is to be thought concerning the absolute and efficacious decree as to Peter's glorification, and concerning the means of grace and of good works through which he will be brought to glory. See this the most learned Báñez, and he exploded consequences of this sort: In these consequences, he says, from the priority of our reason as to the mode of understanding in one kind of cause, a real priority in the things themselves is gathered without any appearance, or the Independence of one thing from another according to the order established by God: as if someone should say, Form was willed by God prior to matter, therefore even if matter were not going to be, form would come to be. These things he, On 1. q. 23 art. 2. Equal is the folly of those who argue: If glory was willed to Peter prior to grace, or prior to the foresight of the good works which flow from grace, then even if Peter remained devoid of grace and of good works, he would nevertheless obtain glory. Away with these ineptitudes! For although God does not will glory to this singular human being from an antecedent intuition of his works, but from the gratuitous good pleasure of his will, yet he wills glory to him with the intuition of future good working, as of a necessary mode, through which God himself ordained that the human being should proceed to obtaining this end.
pass_b_english: Think the same of the absolute, efficacious decree for Peter's glorification, and of the means of grace and good works by which he is brought to glory. Báñez saw this and exploded such consequences (In 1. q.23 a.2): from a priority in our way of understanding one kind of cause, people infer without any show a real priority in the things themselves, or independence of one from another in the order God set — as if: Form was willed by God before matter, therefore form would come to be even if matter never would. Equal folly: If glory was willed to Peter before grace, or before foresight of the good works that flow from grace, then even if Peter stayed devoid of grace and good works he would still get glory. Away with that nonsense! Though God does not will glory to this particular person from prior intuition of his works, but from the gratuitous good pleasure of his will, he still wills him glory with intuition of future good working as the necessary mode by which God ordained that the person proceed to that end.
source_text: Idem prorsus cogitandum de absoluto et efficaci decreto quoad Petri glorificationem, et de mediis gratiae bonorumque operum per quae ad gloriam perducetur. Vide hoc doctissimus Bannes, et hujusmodi consequentias explosit: In istis consequentiis, inquit, ex prioritate nostrae rationis quantum ad modum intelligendi in uno genere causae, colligitur absque ulla apparentia prioritas realis in ipsis rebus, vel Independentia unius rei ab altera secundum ordinem statutum a Deo: sicuti quis diceret, Prius a Deo volita est forma quam materia, ergo etiamsi non esset futura materia, fieret forma. Haec ille, In 1. qu. 23. art. 2. Par illorum stultitia qui argumentantur: Si prius Petro volita sit gloria quam gratia, aut quam praevisa sunt bona opera quae fluunt ex gratia, tum etiamsi Petrus maneret expers gratiae et bonorum operum, gloriam tamen consequeretur. Apage has ineptias! Nam licet Deus non velit gloriam huic singulari homini ex intuitu antecedente operum ejus, sed ex beneplacito voluntatis suae gratuito, vult tamen illi gloriam cum intuitu bonae operationis futurae, tanquam modi necessarii, per quem ipse Deus ordinavit ut ad hunc finem obtinendum homo procederet.
